{{< include ../_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

tidymodels is too large to run in a browser, so these exercises practise the ideas of Chapter 11 with functions that come with R: decision trees with rpart, distances for k-nearest neighbours, and confusion matrices with `table()`. The downloadable project at the bottom uses tidymodels, exactly as in the chapter. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, ex5, ex6]
library(dplyr)
library(rpart)
students      <- read.csv("students.csv")
semesters     <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
questionnaire <- read.csv("questionnaire.csv")
scores <- questionnaire |>
  mutate(
    stress_4 = 6 - stress_4,
    stress   = rowMeans(pick(stress_1:stress_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    burnout  = rowMeans(pick(burnout_1:burnout_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    support  = rowMeans(pick(support_1:support_6), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  select(student_id, stress, burnout, support)
dropout_data <- students |>
  left_join(scores, join_by(student_id)) |>
  left_join(semesters |> filter(semester == 1), join_by(student_id)) |>
  mutate(dropout = factor(considering_dropout, levels = c("Yes", "No"))) |>
  select(dropout, stress, burnout, support, financial_worry, sleep_hours,
         study_hours, wellbeing, gpa) |>
  na.omit()

set.seed(11)
train_rows <- sample(nrow(dropout_data), round(0.75 * nrow(dropout_data)))
train <- dropout_data[train_rows, ]
test  <- dropout_data[-train_rows, ]

model <- glm(dropout == "Yes" ~ stress + burnout + support + financial_worry,
             data = train, family = binomial)
prob  <- predict(model, newdata = test, type = "response")

tiny <- data.frame(
  stress  = c(1.5, 2.0, 2.2, 2.8, 3.0, 3.1, 3.4, 3.6, 3.8, 4.0, 4.2, 4.5),
  support = c(4.5, 3.0, 4.0, 2.0, 4.2, 3.8, 2.1, 4.4, 1.8, 2.5, 3.9, 1.5),
  dropout = factor(c("No", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No",
                     "Yes", "No", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "Yes"))
)
```

## Decision trees

### Exercise 1: The tiny tree

The setup code has created the chapter's twelve imaginary students, `tiny`. Grow a tree that predicts `dropout` from `stress` and `support`, and print it. (`minsplit = 2` lets the tree split even very small groups.)

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
tiny_tree <- rpart(dropout ~ ______ + ______, data = tiny, method = "class",
                   control = rpart.control(minsplit = 2, cp = 0))
tiny_tree
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The two predictors are the two numeric columns of `tiny`.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
tiny_tree <- rpart(dropout ~ stress + support, data = tiny, method = "class",
                   control = rpart.control(minsplit = 2, cp = 0))
tiny_tree
```

The first split is on support (below 2.75), and the second, among the low-support students, on stress (3.1 or more). Every leaf is pure: its `loss` (the number misclassified) is 0.
:::
:::

### Exercise 2: A tree for Elaf's data

Grow a tree of depth 2 on the training data, using all the predictors (`.` means "every other column"), and draw it. Which questions does it ask?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
tree2 <- rpart(dropout ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
               control = rpart.control(maxdepth = ______))
plot(tree2, uniform = TRUE, margin = 0.1)
text(tree2, use.n = TRUE)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
tree2 <- rpart(dropout ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
               control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 2))
plot(tree2, uniform = TRUE, margin = 0.1)
text(tree2, use.n = TRUE)
```

The first question is about support. Only for students with low support does the tree ask a second question, about burnout; students with higher support are all predicted "No". In plain words: students with low support *and* high burnout are the most likely to consider dropping out. The numbers under each leaf are the Yes/No counts of training students.
:::
:::

## k-nearest neighbours

### Exercise 3: Find the nearest neighbours

A new student has a stress score of 2.5 and a support score of 2.2. Calculate the distance from this student to each student in `tiny`, and show the three nearest. What does k-NN with $k = 3$ predict?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
tiny |>
  mutate(distance = sqrt((stress - ______)^2 + (support - ______)^2)) |>
  arrange(distance) |>
  head(3)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
tiny |>
  mutate(distance = sqrt((stress - 2.5)^2 + (support - 2.2)^2)) |>
  arrange(distance) |>
  head(3)
```

The three nearest students have stress 2.8, 3.4, and 2.0, and two of them answered "No", so k-NN predicts "No", with a probability of "Yes" of 1/3. Compare this with the tiny tree from Exercise 1, which says "Yes" only for low support *and* stress of 3.1 or more: it also predicts "No". Different models can agree for some students and disagree for others.
:::
:::

## Evaluating decisions

### Exercise 4: The confusion matrix

The setup code has fitted a logistic regression (`model`) on the training data and stored the predicted probabilities for the test students in `prob`. Classify a student as "Yes" when the probability is 0.5 or more, and cross-tabulate the predictions against the truth.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
predicted <- factor(ifelse(prob >= ______, "Yes", "No"), levels = c("Yes", "No"))
table(predicted, truth = test$______)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
predicted <- factor(ifelse(prob >= 0.5, "Yes", "No"), levels = c("Yes", "No"))
table(predicted, truth = test$dropout)
```

The top-left cell counts the true positives (at-risk students who are flagged), and the bottom-left cell the false negatives (at-risk students who are missed). With a threshold of 0.5, the model misses most of the students at risk.
:::
:::

### Exercise 5: Recall and precision

From the table, calculate the sensitivity (recall: the share of at-risk students who are flagged) and the precision (the share of flagged students who are at risk). Then lower the threshold to 0.2 and calculate them again.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
threshold <- 0.5
predicted <- ifelse(prob >= threshold, "Yes", "No")
truth <- test$dropout
recall    <- sum(predicted == "Yes" & truth == "Yes") / sum(truth == ______)
precision <- sum(predicted == "Yes" & truth == "Yes") / sum(predicted == ______)
c(recall = recall, precision = precision, flagged = mean(predicted == "Yes"))
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Recall divides by all the students who are truly at risk; precision divides by all the students who are flagged.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
threshold <- 0.2
predicted <- ifelse(prob >= threshold, "Yes", "No")
truth <- test$dropout
recall    <- sum(predicted == "Yes" & truth == "Yes") / sum(truth == "Yes")
precision <- sum(predicted == "Yes" & truth == "Yes") / sum(predicted == "Yes")
c(recall = recall, precision = precision, flagged = mean(predicted == "Yes"))
```

Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.2 flags many more students: recall rises a lot, and precision falls. Which threshold is right depends on what happens to a flagged student. For an offer of a conversation with a counsellor, finding more of the students at risk is worth some false alarms.
:::
:::

### Exercise 6: The F1 score

The F1 score combines precision and recall: $F_1 = 2 \times \text{precision} \times \text{recall} / (\text{precision} + \text{recall})$. Write a function for it, and use it on the tiny example from the chapter (precision 8/12, recall 8/10).

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
f1 <- function(precision, recall) {
  ______
}
f1(8/12, 8/10)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex6" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
f1 <- function(precision, recall) {
  2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
}
f1(8/12, 8/10)
```

0.73. The F1 score is always between precision and recall, and closer to the smaller of the two, so it is high only when both are high. Try `f1(0.9, 0.1)`: a model with excellent precision but poor recall gets a low F1.
:::
:::
